 PRO BASKETBALL: IOWANS IN THE NBA 
 Former Hawkeye Bennett Stirtz a perfect fit in OKC 
 Stephen Hunt

 Oklahoma City Thunder guard Bennett Stirtz drives past Dallas Mavericks guard Marcus Sasser during a NBA basketball game Oct. 28, 2026, in Dallas.
 Associated Press 
 DALLAS — Bennett Stirtz knows all about changing teams since the Missouri native went from Northwest Missouri State, where he played two seasons and earned league freshman of the year, to Drake, where he was Missouri Valley newcomer of the year, player of the year and first-team all-conference to Iowa, where he earned first-team All-Big 10 honors in his lone season with the Hawkeyes.
 Now, the affable 23-year-old who was the 16th pick in the 2026 NBA Draft by Memphis, which then traded his rights to Oklahoma City, is five games into his NBA career. And despite again being one of the “new guys,” he has no complaints.
 “Yeah, it’s been super fun. Obviously, different just being in a different environment with new teammates and everything but wouldn’t trade it for the world,” Stirtz said prior to an October 28 game in Dallas. “I’m super blessed. It’s been a super fun year.”
 And one reason he’s fitting in so well and so soon with the Thunder is because of head coach Mark Daigneault.
 “Yeah, I was kind of worried coming in, I didn’t know what NBA head coaches were like and even if they cared about you or anything like that,” Stirtz said. “But yeah, he’s been super good. Went over to his house for dinner. He really cares about you as a person and wants to get to know you. Super down-to-earth person.”
 Stirtz’s lone season in Iowa City saw him average 19.8 points, 4.4 assists, 2.6 rebounds, and 1.4 steals while playing a whopping 37.7 minutes per contest. And even though his time as a Hawkeye was short, it was no less memorable than his previous stops as a collegian.
 “I watched their (the Hawkeyes’) exhibition last night, so it was a little weird watching (with) me not on the team. Super thankful for my time there,” Stirtz said. “All the schools I’ve been to, super grateful for every one of them. The March Madness run for sure (was my favorite memory as a Hawkeye). People from around the nation watching the Hawkeyes in any sport, it’s pretty cool. Seeing the recognition is awesome.”
 One rite of passage for every NBA rookie regardless of their college pedigree is paying their dues in the form of rookie duties. These tasks can arrange from hauling a loud pink backpack around usually with a children’s character like Dora the Explorer all season to announce their rookie status to the world to getting food for veterans, carrying bags, or picking up towels.
 Stirtz already has his main rookie responsibility, one which fellow ex-Hawkeye Jack Dreyer also had several years ago during his rookie season with the Dodgers. “You’ve got to carry the speaker around on the plane. Then, I had to get Krispy Kreme donuts for the plane ride,” he said. “Nothing major. No (I haven’t let the speaker go out), because if I do (let the speaker run out of juice), I know the punishment is something pretty bad and I don’t want to know what it is.”
 Oklahoma City Thunder guard Bennett Stirtz brings the ball up the court during a NBA basketball game against the Dallas Mavericks on Oct. 28 in Dallas.
 Associated Press 
 Like most rookies, the former Hawkeye got his first taste of the Association by playing Summer League right after the draft. In five games, Stirtz averaged 14.4 points, 3.4 assists, 1.6 rebounds, and one steal per game. “I thought it was really good, just playing in a different system because I’d played in the same system for four years. My head’s still kind of spinning around just trying to learn it, but we’re getting there each day,” he said.
 Stirtz has only been a pro for a few months, but he’s already made a strong impression on his new head coach. “He’s got a great mind. He’s got great shooting around the rim. He’s a serious professional and he’s an adult,” Daigneault said. “He’s married, so he takes this thing seriously, knows what he’s doing. Those are generally the types of guys that can improve quickly. Now, he’s going to get the opportunity to do that with minutes and stuff like that. I would expect him to improve pretty quickly here.”
 He’s now part of the fraternity of ex-Hawkeyes in the NBA, a group which currently includes Luka Garza (Boston), Keegan Murray (Sacramento), and Kris Murray (Memphis) and Stirtz can’t wait to catch up with them once the Thunder plays their teams later this season. “Yeah, it’d be fun when you match up with those guys,” Stirtz said. “Talking to those guys after the game when we play them will be pretty fun.”
 He remembers the NBA first entering his mind during his junior season at Drake when agents started calling and trying to sign him. And like many who play at several different schools as collegians, he took positives away from every stop along his basketball journey.
 “Yeah (only spent one year at Iowa), but it’s still a step up, so I think that’s one thing that helped me. I took a step up every year and another one this year. (Playing at three schools) got me ready for this,” Stirtz said.
 Most rookies immediately notice one major difference once they hit the NBA hardwood for the first time and this former Iowa standout is no different. “Yeah, speed of play (is the biggest thing). I would say probably just having an MVP (in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander) and other great players being around each day on the court and not having the ball in your hands as much, that’s probably the biggest difference,” he said.
 And one of those veteran teammates, nine-year veteran Kenrich Williams, has already given him a great bit of sage advice. “Take it in, it goes by super quick,” Stirtz said. “He said it goes by in a flash so you’ve got to take it all in. You’re blessed to be here.”
 When asked whether his welcome to the NBA moment had already occurred, he offered a quick yet appropriate response-stay tuned. “Yeah, specific moment, I still think it’s coming. We’ll have to get back on that one,” Stirtz said.
 IOWANS IN THE NBA
 Former Iowa collegians and Iowa natives who have contributed statistically in NBA games through Sunday:
 Harrison Barnes, San Antonio Spurs — A 15th-year 6-7 forward from North Carolina and Ames is averaging 1.5 points in 4 games.
 Josh Dix, Oklahoma City Thunder — A rookie 6-5 guard from Creighton, Iowa and Council Bluffs is averaging 3 points and 1 rebound in 3 games.
 Luka Garza, Boston Celtics — A sixth-year 6-10 center from Iowa is averaging 5.8 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.2 assists in 6 games.
 AJ Green, Milwaukee Bucks — A fifth-year 6-4 guard from Northern Iowa and Cedar Falls is averaging 6.7 points, 2 threes on 46.2% shooting and 2 rebounds in 6 games.
 Tyrese Haliburton, Indiana Pacers — A seventh-year 6-5 point guard from Iowa State is averaging 21.8 points on 51.6% shooting, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds in 4 games, all starts.
 Joshua Jefferson, Brooklyn Nets — A rookie 6-8 forward from Iowa State is averaging 0 points in 1 game.
 Keegan Murray, Sacramento Kings — A fifth-year 6-8 forward from Iowa and Cedar Rapids Prairie is averaging 7 points, 3 rebounds and 1 steal in 2 games, both starts.
 Kris Murray, Memphis Grizzlies — A fourth-year 6-8 forward from Iowa and Cedar Rapids Prairie is averaging 0.7 points and 1.7 rebounds in 3 games.
 Georges Niang, Golden State Warriors — A 10th-year 6-7 forward from Iowa State is averaging 6.4 points, 2.9 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 7 games, 2 of which were starts.
 Bennett Stirtz, Oklahoma City Thunder — A rookie 6-4 guard from Iowa and Drake is averaging 4.7 points and 1.2 assists in 6 games.
 — Ben Lamparek, The Gazette 
 Stephen Hunt is a freelance writer based in Frisco, Texas
